metadata.title: Lewis v. Casey, 518 U.S. 343 (1996) (No. 94-1511)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Lewis v. Casey

Opinion filed: 1996-06-24

Docket No.: 94-1511

Citations:
• 135 L. Ed. 2d 606
• 116 S. Ct. 2174
• 518 U.S. 343
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 4220

Case holding summaries:
• access-to-courts claim requires showing that the defendants’ conduct caused actual injury to a non-frivolous legal claim
• stating that “the existence of unaddressed jurisdictional defects has no precedential effect”
• access-to-courts claim requires plaintiff to show that the defendants’ conduct caused actual injury to a non-frivolous legal claim
• setting forth elements of an access-to-courts claim and actual injury requirement
• "[S]tanding is not dispensed in gross."
• evaluating the “fundamental con- stitutional right of access to the courts”
• holding prisoner must allege facts showing defendant’s actions hindered his ability to proceed with an actual non- frivolous legal claim
• holding that all access to the courts claims must be based on an actual injury
• “Impairment of any other litigating capacity is simply one of the incidental . . . consequences of conviction and incarceration.”
• access-to-courts claim requires showing that the defendant’s conduct caused actual injury to a non-frivolous legal claim
• “There are further reasons why the order here cannot stand. We held in Turner v. Safley, 482 U.S. 78 (1987), that a prison regulation impinging on inmates’ constitutional rights ‘is valid if it is reasonably related to legitimate penological interests.’” (emphasis added)
• to expand the “right of access” to guaran- tee prisoners a right to “litigate effectively” would essen- tially “demand permanent provision of counsel, which we do not believe the Constitution requires”
• access to courts may be constitutionally curtailed in furtherance of “legitimate penological interests”
• holding that the Constitution does not require the State to "enable the prisoner to discover grievances, and to litigate effectively once in court"
• setting forth elements of an access-to-courts claim and actual injury requirement
• requiring actual injury like prejudice to contemplated or existing litigation for claim of denial of access to courts
• elements of an access- to-courts claim and actual injury requirement
• "[P]rison law libraries and legal assistance 5 programs are not ends in themselves, but only the means for ensuring a reasonably adequate opportunity to present claimed violations of fundamental constitutional rights to the courts."(internal quotations and citation omitted)
• holding that an inmate alleging the denial of meaningful court access must establish not only the inadequacy of legal materials available to him, but also that the alleged shortcomings hindered his efforts to pursue a legal claim
• noting “[i]mpairment of any other litigating capacity is simply one of the incidental (and perfectly constitutional) consequences of conviction and incarceration”
• “Impairment of any other litigating capacity is simply one of the incidental . . . consequences of conviction and incarceration.”
• setting forth elements of an access- to-courts claim and actual injury requirement
• discussing the actual injury requirement
• “[T]he existence of unaddressed jurisdictional defects has no precedential effect.”
• noting that in cases where “standing was neither challenged nor discussed . . . the existence of unaddressed jurisdictional defects has no precedential effect”
• “Depriving someone of a frivolous claim . . . deprives him of nothing at all, except perhaps punishment of . . . sanctions.”
• relying on Bounds v. Smith, 430 U.S. at 830
• stating that a denial of access to the courts claim requires a showing of actual injury
• "[T]he remedy must of course be limited to the [constitutional] inadequacy that produced the injury in fact that the plaintiff has established."
• “Impairment of any other litigating capacity is simply one of the incidental . . . consequences of conviction and incarceration.”
• setting forth actual injury requirement
• setting forth actual injury requirement
• to state an access-to-courts claim, a prisoner must allege “actual injury”
• explaining that an access-to-courts claim requires a plaintiff to show that defendants’ conduct caused an actual injury to a nonfrivolous legal claim
• “[T]he existence of unaddressed juris- dictional defects has no precedential effect.”
• inmate must establish that alleged shortcomings in prison library frustrated a legal claim
• describing the "right of access to the courts" as "already well-established" when Bounds was decided
• plaintiffs with one sort of injury lack standing to challenge a different, though perhaps related, injury, because "standing is not dispensed in gross"
• stating that Wolff "extended the right of access to the courts" to " `civil rights actions' -- i.e., actions under 42 U.S.C. S 1983 to vindicate `basic constitutional rights.' "
• recognizing that the Constitution requires that prisoners be provided the tools "that the inmates need in order to attack their sentences, directly or collaterally, and in order to challenge the conditions of their confinement"
• access-to- courts claim requires showing that the defendant’s conduct caused actual injury to a non-frivolous legal claim
• holding that Bounds did not eliminate the requirement that an inmate allege actual injury that has resulted from a deprivation of adequate legal resources before he can gain standing to sue in federal court
• holding that prisoners could not invoke the access-to-courts right to reform the prison law library without showing that the library’s inadequacies are preventing them from bringing, or caused them to lose, arguable constitutional claims
• observing that “[n]early all of the access-to-courts cases . . . involved attempts by inmates to pursue direct appeals from the convictions for which they were incarcerated . . . habeas petitions, [or] ‘civil rights actions’”
• federal district courts are not to allow themselves to become "enmeshed in the minutiae of prison operations"
• access to courts, encompassing contact with attorney, requires a showing of actual injury, such as prejudice to planned or existing litigation
• prisoners have a right of access to the courts, not to a law library or to legal assistance
• discussing actual-injury requirement as prerequisite to suit alleging violation of fundamental right of access to courts
• to state a claim for denial of access to courts, inmate must show actual prejudice with respect to contemplated or existing litigation
• “Impairment of any other litigating capacity is simply one of the incidental (and perfectly constitutional) consequences of conviction and incarceration.”
